```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
import math
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("..").resolve()
man = json.loads((root / "exports" / "data" / "cad_manifest.json").read_text())
L = man["layout"]
des = json.loads((root / "exports" / "data" / "design_derivations.json").read_text())
DA = des["auger"]
LB = lambda k: des["ledger"][k]["value"]
MA = des["mast"]
MG = MA["geometry_m"]
import yaml
_cfg = yaml.safe_load((root / "config" / "system_params.yaml").read_text())
p_bit = _cfg["drill_bit"]
P_ROT = _cfg["actuators"]["rotary"]
A = man["assemblies"]
N = man["nodes"]

def emit_html(html_str: str) -> None:
    print(f"\n```{{=html}}\n{html_str.strip()}\n```\n")

def size_mm(name: str) -> str:
    (x0, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z1) = A[name]["bbox_mm"]
    return f"{x1 - x0:.0f} &times; {y1 - y0:.0f} &times; {z1 - z0:.0f} mm"

FORMATS = [
    ("step", "STEP", "exact B-rep, assembly tree, mm"),
    ("stl", "STL", "triangle mesh, mm"),
    ("glb", "glTF binary (.glb)", "web mesh with materials, m"),
]

def downloads(name):
    items = "".join(f'<a href="assets/cad/{name}.{ext}" download><strong>{lab}</strong><span>{note}</span></a>' for ext, lab, note in FORMATS)
    return f'<details class="cad-dl"><summary>Download</summary><div class="cad-dl-menu">{items}</div></details>'

def card(name, title, orbit, alt, extra_attrs=""):
    """Viewer card only: header, model, download menu. The explanation is written outside the card."""
    return f"""
  <figure class="cad-card">
    <div class="cad-card-header">
      <div><h4>{title}</h4><span class="cad-tag">{A[name]['parts']} parts &middot; envelope {size_mm(name)}</span></div>
      {downloads(name)}
    </div>
    <model-viewer src="assets/cad/{name}.glb" alt="{alt}" camera-controls touch-action="pan-y"
      environment-image="neutral" tone-mapping="neutral" shadow-intensity="0.55" shadow-softness="0.9" exposure="0.75"
      camera-orbit="{orbit}" interaction-prompt="none" loading="eager" {extra_attrs}>
      <div class="cad-load-error" slot="error">Model failed to load. Serve the site over HTTP; browsers block <code>.glb</code> files opened directly from disk.</div>
    </model-viewer>
  </figure>"""

def notes(bullets):
    return '<ul class="cad-notes">' + "".join(f"<li>{b}</li>" for b in bullets) + "</ul>"

def subsection(heading, cards, bullets, lead=""):
    print(f"\n### {heading}\n")
    if lead:
        print(f"\n{lead}\n")
    grid = "cad-viewer-grid" if len(cards) > 1 else "cad-viewer-single"
    emit_html(f'<div class="{grid}">' + "".join(cards) + "</div>")
    emit_html(notes(bullets))

CC = man["colour_code"]
LAYC = _cfg["cad_layout"]
r_ex = L["auger_od_mm"] / 2
delta_ex, ang_ex = 0.08, 0.25
theta_dev = 2 * math.acos(1 - delta_ex / r_ex)
n_seg = math.ceil(2 * math.pi / min(theta_dev, ang_ex))
HOME = man["kinematics"]["home_tip_m"]
STROKE = HOME + 1.0
GOVERNS = "the angular limit governs" if ang_ex < theta_dev else "the deviation limit governs"
N_TEL = len((root / "exports" / "data" / "telemetry_moon.csv").open().readline().strip().split(","))
SEARCH = _cfg["actuators"]["z_axis_feed"]
```

Each component on this page is a solid model generated from the system's design parameters, not drawn by hand. Its dimensions come from the physics-based sizing (loads, stresses, fatigue, vibration and thermal limits), and the browser shows the result as an interactive 3D model.

A **boundary representation (B-rep)** describes a solid by the surfaces that enclose it. It stores the faces (pieces of planes, cylinders, cones, tori or NURBS surfaces), the edges where faces meet and the vertices where edges meet, together with the topology that records which face borders which [@requicha1980; @stroud2006brep; @piegl1997nurbs]. Because the boundary is exact, a bearing bore is a true cylinder of a known diameter, and volume, mass, centre of gravity and moments of inertia follow directly from the geometry. A B-rep model is **parametric** when every dimension is an expression of named inputs, such as auger diameter, flight pitch, bearing size or mast section, instead of a fixed number [@shah1995parametric]. When a derivation changes a value (for example the flute depth set by the fatigue check), the solids rebuild with the new value and every dependent dimension follows.

An **application programming interface (API)** is the set of functions that one piece of software publishes so that other programs can use it. **WebGL** is such an interface: a JavaScript API, standardised by the Khronos Group, through which a web page sends triangles, material colours and lights to the computer's graphics processor (GPU) [@webgl2]. The viewers on this page use it to draw each model at interactive frame rates in any modern browser, with no plug-in.

The models are published in three file formats, each suited to a different task:

- **STEP** (ISO 10303-21) is the neutral exchange format for engineering CAD [@iso10303_21]. It carries the exact B-rep geometry, the assembly tree, part names and colours, and it opens in any major CAD package for further design, analysis or manufacture.
- **STL** stores only a list of flat triangles and their normals, with no units, colours or assembly structure [@stl1988]. It is the usual input for 3D printing and for many meshing tools.
- **glTF** (GL Transmission Format) is the Khronos format for delivering 3D scenes to real-time renderers, and **GLB** is its single-file binary form [@gltf2]. It holds triangle meshes, physically based material properties and a hierarchy of nodes, and it is the format the viewers below load.

## Modelling approach

Every part is modelled once as a parametric B-rep solid by the CAD generator, sized from the same parameter set and design derivations used in the sizing calculations. The same solids are written to colour-labelled, assembly-structured STEP files (mm), tessellated to STL (mm), and tessellated to glTF `.glb` (m, Y-up) for the viewers below. The web models and the engineering STEP files therefore always match.

**Tessellation.** The STEP file keeps the exact curved surfaces, but a GPU or a 3D printer can only process flat triangles. Tessellation replaces each curved face by a mesh of triangles whose vertices lie on the true surface, so each triangle edge is a chord across the curve. The error is the chordal deviation, the largest gap between a triangle and the surface it replaces. For a face of radius $r$ divided into segments that each span an angle $\theta$:

$$
\delta = r\left(1 - \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right)
$$

::: {.symbols}
- $\delta$: chordal deviation, the largest distance between the true surface and the triangle that replaces it (mm)
- $r$: local radius of curvature of the face (mm)
- $\theta$: angle one segment spans at the centre of curvature (rad)
:::

The generator holds $\delta \le$ `{python} f"{delta_ex:.2f}"` mm and $\theta \le$ `{python} f"{ang_ex:.2f}"` rad. On the `{python} f"{r_ex:.0f}"` mm radius of the auger flight, the deviation limit alone would allow $\theta =$ `{python} f"{theta_dev:.3f}"` rad, so `{python} GOVERNS` and a full circle becomes `{python} f"{n_seg}"` segments. The worst-case error is `{python} f"{100 * delta_ex / r_ex:.1f}"` % of the radius, below what a screen can show and below ordinary machining tolerances. Thin, repeated features (helical flights, bristle tufts, coil springs) use coarser limits to keep the files small. The web copy is also converted to the glTF convention of metres with $+Y$ up [@gltf2]: a CAD point $(x, y, z)$ in millimetres with $Z$ up becomes $(x,\ z,\ -y)\times10^{-3}$ m. That is a rotation of $-90^\circ$ about the $x$-axis followed by a scale, so the frame stays right-handed and lengths, angles and the hand of every helix are preserved.

**Home pose.** The rig is drawn at 1:1 scale in its *home* pose, the reference configuration from which every motion is measured. In robot-kinematics terms it is the zero position of the prismatic feed joint [@craig2005robotics]. The carriage sits at the top of its travel on the rails, so the drill string is fully withdrawn and the bit tip hangs `{python} f"{HOME * 1000:.0f}"` mm above the regolith. That height clears the mast foot plate (`{python} f"{LAYC['foot_top_m'] * 1000:.0f}"` mm) and the top of the brush (about `{python} f"{LAYC['brush_axle_height_m'] * 1000 + L['brush_tip_radius_mm']:.0f}"` mm), so the parked bit touches neither the brushing station nor the ground and the load cell reads no weight on bit. To reach the 1.0 m target depth the carriage therefore needs a stroke of `{python} f"{HOME:.2f}"` + 1.00 = `{python} f"{STROKE:.2f}"` m. A mission starts and ends here: the controller leaves home, approaches at `{python} f"{SEARCH['search_speed_m_s'] * 1000:.0f}"` mm/s until the load cell detects `{python} f"{SEARCH['contact_detect_wob_n']:.0f}"` N of contact, and returns to home after the last bite. The digital twin moves the carriage by the displacement $\Delta z = z_\text{tip} - z_\text{home}$ from this pose.

::: {.symbols}
- $\Delta z$: carriage displacement from the home pose, positive upward (m)
- $z_\text{tip}$: bit-tip height above the regolith surface at the current instant, negative once the bit is in the hole (m)
- $z_\text{home}$: bit-tip height in the home pose, `{python} f"{HOME:.2f}"` m
:::

**Colour code.** The colours carry engineering meaning. Each part is coloured by the job it does in the machine, so a load or energy path can be traced by eye, as in the cutaway drawings of engineering manuals. Finishes are matte, in the manner of technical illustration, so that hue rather than mirror-like highlights carries the information [@gooch1998]. The eight function hues are the Okabe–Ito colour-universal-design set, chosen so the classes stay distinguishable for readers with colour-vision deficiency, about one man in twelve [@okabe2008cud; @wong2011color]. Two neutral greys mark the primary structure and the lander. The same colours are written into the STEP part labels, so the code carries into any CAD package.

```{python}
#| output: asis
rows_cc = "".join(
    f'<tr><td><span class="cc-swatch" style="background:{c["hex"]}"></span></td><td><strong>{c["label"]}</strong></td><td>{c["function"]}</td></tr>'
    for c in CC
)
emit_html(f"""<div class="mbse-table-wrap"><table class="mbse-table cc-table">
<thead><tr><th>Colour</th><th>Function class</th><th>Parts and role</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>{rows_cc}</tbody></table></div>""")
```

Read together, the classes follow the energy through the machine: electrical power is converted in the motors (blue), carried as torque and feed force through the drive train (orange) or stored and released as impact in the percussion path (vermillion), delivered to the rock by the carbide (black), and the reactions return to the lander through the structure (greys). A part's class follows its role, not its material: the bronze leadscrew nut is orange because it transmits feed force, while the bronze chute is green because it carries the sample.

In every viewer below, drag to orbit, scroll to zoom and right-drag to pan. The tag under each title gives the part count and the overall envelope (width &times; depth &times; height). The **Download** menu offers each model in the three file formats.

## Integrated drill rig and kinematic structure

```{python}
#| output: asis
emit_html('<div class="cad-viewer-single cad-viewer-tall">' + card(
    "full_drill_rig", "Complete drill rig, home pose", "-25deg 75deg auto", "Complete drill rig") + "</div>")
```

The complete assembly brings every subassembly above onto the lander at its true position. It is stored as a **scene graph**: a tree of nodes, each holding a coordinate frame (a position and an orientation relative to its *parent node*) and the parts attached to that frame [@foley1990]. A node inherits every motion of its parent and adds its own. A part's pose in the world is therefore the product of the transforms along the path from the root of the tree to the node that holds it:

$$
\mathbf{T}_\text{world} = \mathbf{T}_1\,\mathbf{T}_2 \cdots \mathbf{T}_n
$$

::: {.symbols}
- $\mathbf{T}_\text{world}$: $4\times4$ homogeneous transform giving the part's position (m) and orientation in the world frame
- $\mathbf{T}_1 \ldots \mathbf{T}_n$: transform of each node relative to its parent, from the root ($1$) down to the node that holds the part ($n$); each combines a $3\times3$ rotation and a translation (m)
:::

This is the forward-kinematics rule used for serial robot arms [@craig2005robotics]. The tree follows the physical joints of the machine: parts that are bolted together share one node, because a rigid body has a single pose, and a new node starts wherever a joint lets one group move relative to another. The solar wings show the nesting most clearly. Each elevation node is the child of an azimuth node, which is the child of the static power-system node, so turning a turntable carries the yoke and panels round with it, and the elevation tilt is then applied in the turned frame, exactly as in a two-axis gimbal. The drill-head nodes (carriage, auger, hammer, cam) sit side by side under the root and receive the same feed displacement, which is equivalent to a rigid attachment to the carriage. With this structure, one number per joint is enough to pose the whole machine.

The numbers come from **state-machine telemetry**. The drill's autonomy software is a finite-state machine: at every instant it is in exactly one of six states (IDLE, ACTIVE, SEARCH, DRILL, RETRACTION, TRANSFER) and it moves to another only when a defined physical condition is met [@harel1987statecharts]. For example, SEARCH becomes DRILL when the load cell reads the contact force, and DRILL becomes RETRACTION when the bite reaches its length or when a temperature or torque limit trips. The mission simulation steps this machine forward once per second, solving the cutting mechanics, the bit's heat balance and the sun geometry at each step. It records the result as telemetry, a time series of `{python} f"{N_TEL}"` columns that include bit-tip depth, weight on bit, spindle speed and torque, percussion duty, bit temperature, sun azimuth and elevation, and carousel station. The digital twin on the Results &amp; Digital Twin page [@grieves2017twin] reads this record and turns each channel into a joint coordinate: depth sets the carriage translation, spindle speed is integrated over time into the auger's spin angle, the sun angles set the wing gimbals and the bite counter sets the carousel index. The animation is therefore a replay of what the simulated controller did, not a scripted sequence.

```{python}
#| output: asis
dof = {
    "Frame_Node": "Static. Lander deck, legs, hinge, latch posts and the deployed mast, latched on its posts.",
    "Solar_Node": "Static. Tanks, warm box, outriggers and turntable housings.",
    "Solar_Wing_Port_Az_Node": "Azimuth rotation about the turntable axis, following the computed sun azimuth.",
    "Solar_Wing_Port_Elev_Node": "Elevation tilt about the yoke axis, so the cell normal follows the sun elevation.",
    "Solar_Wing_Starboard_Az_Node": "As port.",
    "Solar_Wing_Starboard_Elev_Node": "As port.",
    "Carriage_Node": f"Vertical translation along the rails: {(man['kinematics']['home_tip_m'] + 1.0):.2f} m stroke (home &rarr; 1.0 m bit depth).",
    "Auger_Node": "Same translation as the carriage, plus spin about the auger axis at the commanded RPM.",
    "Hammer_Cam_Node": f"Carriage translation, plus spindle rotation (splined hammer) and a {des['hammer']['blow_frequency_hz']:.0f} Hz cam-lift / drop stroke while percussing.",
    "Cam_Ring_Node": "Carriage translation, plus barrel-cam spin while percussing.",
    "Brush_Gear_Node": f"Worm-wheel spin about its own axle: one tuft per auger revolution ({LB('brush_speed_ratio')}:1), plus the axial auger speed over the {LB('brush_pitch_radius_mm'):.0f} mm pitch radius.",
    "Carousel_Node": f"Index rotation about the carousel axis under the foot plate: one station ({360 / LB('carousel_stations'):.1f}&deg;) per bite, so bite n always fills cup n.",
}
rows = "\n".join(
    f"<tr><td><code>{k}</code></td><td>{len(v)}</td><td>{', '.join(n.replace('_', ' ') for n in v[:6])}{' &hellip;' if len(v) > 6 else ''}</td><td>{dof[k]}</td></tr>"
    for k, v in N.items()
)
emit_html(f"""
<div class="mbse-table-wrap">
  <table class="mbse-table">
    <thead><tr><th>glTF node</th><th>Parts</th><th>Contents</th><th>Motion in the digital twin</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>{rows}</tbody>
  </table>
</div>
""")
```

The table lists each node of the scene graph: how many parts it carries, what they are, and the motion the digital twin gives it. Two nodes are static. The frame node (lander deck, legs, hinge, latch and the deployed, latched mast) and the power-system base carry loads but do not move while drilling. Counting the remaining joints gives the mobility of the machine. **Eight coordinates are independent**, each driven by its own actuator: the carriage feed (a prismatic joint, leadscrew motor), the spindle rotation (rotary motor), the barrel-cam rotation (percussion motor), the carousel index (stepper) and the azimuth and elevation of both solar wings (four gimbal motors). **The other motions are dependent**, fixed by kinematic constraints rather than by motors. The auger, hammer and cam translate with the carriage. The hammer turns with the spindle through its spline and rises and drops as a function of the cam angle. The brush has no motor at all: it is a worm wheel meshing with the auger flight, so its speed follows from the flight lead and the motion of the string,

$$
\omega_b = \frac{1}{r_p}\left(\frac{\omega_a\,p}{2\pi} + v_z\right)
$$

::: {.symbols}
- $\omega_b$: angular speed of the brush (rad/s)
- $r_p$: pitch radius of the brush tufts, `{python} f"{LB('brush_pitch_radius_mm'):.1f}"` mm
- $\omega_a$: angular speed of the auger (rad/s)
- $p$: lead of the flight passing the brush, `{python} f"{L['sampling_pitch_mm']:.1f}"` mm in the sampling zone and `{python} f"{L['transport_pitch_mm']:.1f}"` mm in the transport zone
- $v_z$: axial speed of the string past the brush (m/s)
:::

This split between independent and dependent motions is why the controller needs only eight commanded set-points to pose a `{python} f"{A['full_drill_rig']['parts']}"`-part machine. The barrel cam's spin is drawn at a reduced rate so it stays readable. The hammer stroke is drawn at the true blow rate of `{python} f"{des['hammer']['blow_frequency_hz']:.0f}"` Hz, which a 60 Hz display can only just resolve: about `{python} f"{60 / des['hammer']['blow_frequency_hz']:.1f}"` frames per blow, against the minimum of two samples per cycle set by the sampling theorem [@shannon1949].
